lead: Network synthesis is analysis run backwards. Analysis finds the driving-point impedance Z(s) of a given circuit; synthesis starts with Z(s), asks whether passive R, L and C can produce it, and builds the circuit. Z(s) must be positive real, and for LC or RC networks its poles and zeros must follow a strict pattern. Foster's method then builds the network by partial fractions and Cauer's by continued fractions, giving four standard circuits with the same impedance.
prereq: You need the Laplace transform, network functions with their poles and zeros, and the impedances sL, 1/(sC) and R of the three elements.

sections.h3: Driving-point functions and the positive-real test

blocks.text: A driving-point impedance Z(s) = V(s)/I(s) is measured at one port, with zero initial conditions; the driving-point admittance is Y(s) = 1/Z(s). For R, L and C it is a ratio of two polynomials in s with real, non-negative coefficients.

Z(s) can be built from passive elements only if it is positive real (PR): (1) Z(s) is real when s is real, and (2) Re Z(s) ≥ 0 whenever Re s ≥ 0. For a rational function this is tested in three steps:

items: The numerator and denominator are Hurwitz polynomials (no roots in the right half plane), so Z(s) has no poles or zeros with Re s > 0.
Poles on the jω axis (including s = 0 and s = ∞) are simple, with real, positive residues.

blocks.text: The degrees of numerator and denominator differ by at most one. Condition 3 says the one-port can only absorb average power. Every PR function can be built from R, L, C and coupled coils (Brune's method).

An LC (lossless, reactance) function is an odd rational function: even polynomial over odd, or odd over even, with degrees differing by exactly one. Its poles and zeros are simple, lie on the jω axis, and alternate; s = 0 and s = ∞ are always critical frequencies (a pole or a zero). Its partial fractions are

blocks.where: where k∞, k₀ and every kᵢ are positive (or zero for the first two). Re Z(jω) = 0 everywhere, and the reactance X(ω) always rises with ω.

blocks.text: An RC impedance has simple, alternating poles and zeros on the negative real axis (s = −σ). The critical frequency nearest the origin is a pole (possibly at s = 0) and the one farthest away is a zero (possibly at ∞), so Z(0) > Z(∞). Its expansion is Z(s) = K∞ + K₀/s + Σ Kᵢ/(s + σᵢ) with all constants positive.

Foster I expands Z(s) in partial fractions: the terms are elements in series. For LC, k∞s is an inductor L = k∞, k₀/s a capacitor C = 1/k₀, and 2kᵢs/(s² + ωᵢ²) a parallel LC tank with C = 1/(2kᵢ) and L = 2kᵢ/ωᵢ². Foster II expands Y(s): the terms are branches in parallel; k∞s is a capacitor, k₀/s an inductor, and 2kᵢs/(s² + ωᵢ²) a series LC branch with L = 1/(2kᵢ) and C = 2kᵢ/ωᵢ².

Cauer I removes the pole at infinity again and again by long division with the polynomials in descending powers. Each quotient is a series inductor or a shunt capacitor, giving a ladder. Cauer II removes the pole at s = 0 again and again by dividing with the polynomials in ascending powers, giving series capacitors and shunt inductors. Every form of an LC function uses the same number of elements, equal to the highest power of s in the function.

figure.caption: The LC impedance of the worked example: its poles (×) and zeros (○) alternate along the jω axis, so it is realizable. Partial fractions give the Foster I chain and long division gives the Cauer I ladder; both have four elements.

spec.aria: A frequency axis with poles at 0, root 2 and infinity and zeros at 1 and root 3, alternating. Below, Foster I: 1 H, 2/3 F and a tank of 1/4 H parallel 2 F in series. Below that, Cauer I: series 1 H, shunt 1/2 F, series 4 H, shunt 1/6 F.

examples.question: Show that Z(s) = (s² + 1)(s² + 3)/[s(s² + 2)] is an LC impedance and realize it in Foster I, Foster II, Cauer I and Cauer II forms.
steps: Poles: s = 0, ±j√2 (1.414) and s = ∞ (numerator degree 4, denominator 3). Zeros: ±j1 and ±j√3 (1.732). Along the jω axis: pole 0, zero 1, pole 1.414, zero 1.732, pole ∞. They alternate, all are simple, and Z is even over odd: an LC impedance.
Foster I. k∞ = 1 (leading coefficients). k₀ = [sZ(s)] at s = 0 = 3/2. At s² = −2: (s² + 2)Z/s = (s⁴ + 4s² + 3)/s² = (4 − 8 + 3)/(−2) = 1/2 = 2k₁. So Z = s + 1.5/s + 0.5s/(s² + 2).
Foster I elements, all in series: L = 1 H, C = 1/1.5 = 2/3 F, and a tank with C = 1/0.5 = 2 F and L = 0.5/2 = 1/4 H.

Foster II. Y = s(s² + 2)/[(s² + 1)(s² + 3)] = 0.5s/(s² + 1) + 0.5s/(s² + 3) (residues 1/2 at s² = −1 and at s² = −3). Two series LC branches in parallel: L = 1/0.5 = 2 H with C = 0.5/1 = 1/2 F, and L = 2 H with C = 0.5/3 = 1/6 F.

Cauer I (descending powers): (s⁴ + 4s² + 3) ÷ (s³ + 2s) gives s, remainder 2s² + 3 → series L₁ = 1 H. (s³ + 2s) ÷ (2s² + 3) gives s/2, remainder s/2 → shunt C₂ = 1/2 F. (2s² + 3) ÷ (s/2) gives 4s, remainder 3 → series L₃ = 4 H. (s/2) ÷ 3 gives s/6 → shunt C₄ = 1/6 F.

Cauer II (ascending powers): (3 + 4s² + s⁴) ÷ (2s + s³) gives 3/(2s), remainder 2.5s² + s⁴ → series C₁ = 2/3 F. (2s + s³) ÷ (2.5s² + s⁴) gives 4/(5s), remainder 0.2s³ → shunt L₂ = 5/4 H. (2.5s² + s⁴) ÷ 0.2s³ gives 25/(2s), remainder s⁴ → series C₃ = 2/25 F. 0.2s³ ÷ s⁴ gives 1/(5s) → shunt L₄ = 5 H.
Check: at s = j1 Foster I gives j(1 − 1.5 + 0.5) = 0, the expected zero at ω = 1 rad/s.
examples.answer: Foster I: 1 H, 2/3 F and a 1/4 H ∥ 2 F tank in series. Foster II: (2 H, 1/2 F) and (2 H, 1/6 F) series branches in parallel. Cauer I: series 1 H, shunt 1/2 F, series 4 H, shunt 1/6 F. Cauer II: series 2/3 F, shunt 5/4 H, series 2/25 F, shunt 5 H. Each uses four elements.

examples.question: Show that Z(s) = (s + 2)(s + 4)/[(s + 1)(s + 3)] is an RC impedance and realize it in Foster I form.
steps: From the origin: pole −1, zero −2, pole −3, zero −4. They alternate on the negative real axis and the nearest is a pole: an RC impedance. Z(0) = 8/3 Ω > Z(∞) = 1 Ω ✓.
A term K/(s + σ) is a parallel RC: Z = (1/C)/(s + 1/(RC)), so C = 1/K and R = K/σ.
Check at s = 0: 1 + 1.5 + 1/6 = 2.667 Ω = Z(0) ✓ (every capacitor open, the resistors in series).
examples.answer: A 1 Ω resistor in series with (1.5 Ω ∥ 2/3 F) and (1/6 Ω ∥ 2 F).

traps: Positive coefficients alone do not make a function PR or LC. Z(s) = (s² + 4)/[s(s² + 1)] has positive coefficients, but its critical frequencies run pole 0, pole 1, zero 2; its residue at ±j1 is −3, so it is not an LC impedance.
(s² + 4)/(s² + 1) is not an LC impedance: it is even, and Re Z(jω) < 0 between 1 and 2 rad/s, so it is not even PR.
Foster I expands Z(s) into series elements; Foster II expands Y(s) into parallel branches. Expanding Y but drawing series elements gives the dual circuit, not the asked one.
In Foster I a term k₀/s is a capacitor of 1/k₀, not k₀: 1.5/s is 2/3 F.
For an RC impedance the critical frequency nearest the origin must be a pole. (s + 1)/(s + 2) has a zero nearest the origin, so it is an RL impedance (or an RC admittance), not an RC impedance.

quiz.q: State the conditions for a rational Z(s) to be positive real.
quiz.a: Z(s) is real for real s; it has no poles or zeros in the right half plane; poles on the jω axis are simple with positive real residues; and Re Z(jω) ≥ 0 for all ω.

quiz.q: Why must the poles and zeros of an LC impedance alternate?
quiz.a: The reactance X(ω) of an LC one-port always rises with frequency. Between two poles X runs from −∞ up to +∞, so it must cross zero once; between two zeros it must pass through a pole. So they interlace.

quiz.q: Realize Z(s) = (s² + 1)/[s(s² + 4)] in Foster I form.
quiz.a: k₀ = 1/4 and, at s² = −4, (s² + 1)/s² = 3/4, so Z = 0.25/s + 0.75s/(s² + 4). Elements in series: C = 1/0.25 = 4 F and a tank with C = 1/0.75 = 4/3 F, L = 0.75/4 = 3/16 H.

quiz.q: Realize the same Z(s) = (s² + 1)/[s(s² + 4)] in Cauer I form.
quiz.a: Z has a zero at ∞, so start with Y = (s³ + 4s)/(s² + 1). Divide: s, remainder 3s → shunt C = 1 F. (s² + 1) ÷ 3s = s/3, remainder 1 → series L = 1/3 H. 3s ÷ 1 = 3s → shunt C = 3 F.

quiz.q: Can Z(s) = 2(s + 3)/(s + 1) be an RC impedance? If so, realize it.
quiz.a: Yes: pole −1 nearest the origin, zero −3 beyond it, Z(0) = 6 Ω > Z(∞) = 2 Ω. Z = 2 + 4/(s + 1): a 2 Ω resistor in series with a parallel RC of R = 4 Ω and C = 1/4 F.

beyond: Not for the exam. Passive Butterworth and Chebyshev filters are Cauer-type ladders with tabulated element values, and active RC filters replace the inductors with op-amps. Search for “Cauer ladder filter” and “Foster reactance theorem”.
